title: Listening with the words
hook: follow the Gurmukhi and its meaning as the hymn is sung

segments.voice: Yesterday, rahao, the pause line at a hymn's center. Your line was pause here. Did you let one important sentence land? Day one hundred eight.

A film in a language you don't speak, with subtitles. At first the eyes race along the bottom of the screen and miss the faces. Then something shifts: the actor's voice breaks at the same moment the words go by, and the two lock together. Not reading, not listening, but both at once, and the scene hits twice as hard. In many gurdwaras today there's something similar. On a screen near the front, as the hymn is sung, the Gurmukhi words appear line by line, and under them, the sounds in English letters, and under that, a translation.
screen: `SUBTITLES THAT CLICK.` → `THE VOICE AND THE WORDS LOCK.` → `THE SCREEN NEAR THE FRONT.`

segments.voice: For four days you've practiced listening: just listening, then the mood of the raag, then the instruments, then the rahao line. Today adds the words. The practice is simple: as a shabad is sung, follow along with it. The Gurmukhi if you can read it, the sounds if you can't, and the meaning either way. Sound and sense together. Why bother? Because for Sikhs, the music is never just music. Guru Ram Das says it in the Guru Granth Sahib. In paraphrase: the Word is the Guru, and the Guru is the Word, and within the Word is all the nectar. The raag carries the mood; the words carry the teaching. When you hear both at once, the hymn can reach all of you. Here's what often happens the first time you try. You lose your place. The singer repeats a line you weren't expecting, or jumps back to the rahao, and your eyes are three lines behind. That's normal. Kirtan repeats on purpose. Let the rahao be your anchor: when you're lost, look for it, because the singers will come back to it. Some Sikhs who grew up outside Punjab say this is how they came to know the Granth. Not in a classroom, but on a Sunday morning, reading along with the screen, line by line, year after year, until one day a line in Gurmukhi meant something without the translation. And you don't need the gurdwara to do this. Apps and websites show the Gurmukhi, the sounds and a translation together, and many recordings are easy to follow along with.
screen: `FOUR DAYS OF LISTENING, THEN WORDS.` · `THE WORD IS THE GURU.` · `LOST? FIND THE RAHAO.` · `LINE BY LINE, YEAR AFTER YEAR.` · then, large: `SOUND AND SENSE TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: If you can, play one shabad and open its words beside it, in Gurmukhi, in English letters, and in translation. Follow along once. Let your eyes move with the voice. When you lose your place, don't stop the music. Look for the rahao line and wait for it to come back. If you can't play one right now, read a single line of a shabad aloud, slowly, then read its meaning, then say the line again. The bell holds the time.
Listening with the words. Following a shabad's Gurmukhi and its meaning while it's sung, so the sound and the sense arrive together.
Your line: sound and sense together. Today, read along once with one hymn or one song, and notice the moment the words and the music lock. Day one hundred eight.

howItsDone: Many gurdwaras display the words of the shabad being sung on a screen, in Gurmukhi with transliteration and translation, and Sikhs at home often follow along using apps or printed gutkas.

fork.reveal: the rahao is the anchor. the singers keep coming back to it, so you can always find your place again.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: the Guru's word, the hymns of the Granth.

trapdoor: what you thought: reading the lyrics.
what it means: following the sung Word with its meaning, so the music carries the teaching into you.
what a scholar hears: Guru Ram Das's line that the Word is the Guru and the Guru the Word (Ang 982), and the modern gurdwara practice of projected Gurmukhi, transliteration and translation.
